vignette:
He is 53, a South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life working as a painter, the kind of tradesman who notices shades other people miss. He talks easily about color-how a wall can look warm or cold depending on the hour, how a careful hand can make an old room feel new-but when the conversation turns to the years of war, his voice becomes flatter, as if he is describing someone else's life.

He grows up in a city where ordinary routines slowly become organized around danger. At first there are distant explosions, rumors, checkpoints, streets to avoid. Then the violence moves closer, until daily life is shaped by calculation: when to leave the house, which road is less exposed, how long to stay at the market. He is a young husband then, newly responsible not only for himself but for his wife and, later, their children. He keeps working when he can, taking painting jobs in damaged buildings and private homes, carrying brushes and cans past shattered concrete and windows blown out by blasts. He tells himself that if he keeps earning, if he keeps moving, then life is still life.

The moment he returns to most often begins as an ordinary workday. He is painting inside a residential building, standing on a ladder, focused on cutting a clean line where the wall meets the ceiling. He remembers the smell of thinner, the radio playing faintly somewhere downstairs, the irritation of paint drying too fast in the heat. Then there is a deafening blast that seems to come through his whole body before he understands what it is. The building shudders. Glass bursts inward. He falls from the ladder and lands hard, ears ringing, mouth full of dust. For a few seconds he cannot see. He thinks the room has gone dark, but it is the powder in the air.

Outside, people are screaming. He runs down the stairs and into a street he no longer recognizes. There is smoke, twisted metal, blood on the pavement, someone calling for a child. He does what others are doing-lifting debris, carrying the injured, shouting names-but later what stays with him is not the sequence of events so much as fragments: a sandal without its owner, a hand pressed to a wound, the smell of burning mixed with wet cement. He does not know how close he came to dying. He only knows that from that day on, his body behaves as if the blast is always about to happen again.

Even after he and his family leave the war zone, he does not feel as if he has arrived anywhere safe. In the new country, he finds work painting apartments, hallways, offices. On the surface he is dependable and skilled. He comes early, lays down drop cloths carefully, works in silence, and leaves spaces cleaner than he found them. But his days are organized around vigilance. He scans stairwells and parking lots before entering. Sudden bangs-a door slamming, a tool dropped on concrete, a truck backfiring-hit him with a jolt so strong that his knees weaken and his heart races. For a moment he is back in that building, swallowing dust. He feels embarrassed when coworkers notice him flinch, so he laughs it off or says he is tired.

At home, his wife experiences him as present but far away. He loves his family deeply, but he is often on edge, especially in crowded settings. He prefers to sit facing the door in restaurants and grows tense if his children, now older, are late coming home. He checks locks more than once before bed. Sleep is unreliable. Some nights he lies awake listening for sounds he cannot name; other nights he wakes abruptly from dreams in which walls shake and he is trying, unsuccessfully, to reach someone through smoke. His wife tells him he sometimes shouts in his sleep. In the morning he minimizes it, washes his face, and goes to work.

He avoids news about war, but images still find him. A television clip, a siren, even the smell of plaster dust at a demolition site can pull up memories he tries hard not to touch. He has become practiced at narrowing his world: work, home, familiar routes, familiar people. He says little about the past because once he starts to remember, the memories do not come like stories. They come like pieces of the event itself-physical, immediate, unfinished.

What troubles him almost as much as fear is the change in his inner life. He used to think of himself as sociable, patient, steady with his hands and with people. Now he notices how quickly irritation rises in him, how often he wants to withdraw. On weekends, when there is no job to focus on, he feels restless and heavy at the same time. He sometimes stands in front of a wall he has just painted and stares at it longer than necessary, appreciating the smoothness, the repaired surface, the evidence that damage can be covered. Even then, he knows there are cracks underneath that careful work, and he lives with the sense that something in him still listens for the next blast.
